questions.question: Explain why and how the British took control of the Cape.
questions.expected_answer: The VOC was bankrupt (dissolved 1799); France occupied the Netherlands (Batavian Republic, 1795); Britain feared France would use the Cape to threaten the sea route to India. First British Occupation 1795-1803 (after a skirmish at Muizenberg); returned to the Batavian Republic under the Treaty of Amiens (1803-1806); Second British Occupation after the Battle of Blaauwberg (January 1806); formally ceded in 1814.

questions.question: Describe the changes the British introduced at the Cape, including laws affecting the Khoikhoi.
questions.expected_answer: Anglicisation: English official for government (1822) and courts (1828), British currency, circuit courts (1811), rule by appointed governors (e.g. Caledon, Cradock, Somerset), Legislative Council (1834); end of VOC monopolies, British trade, wine then wool exports. Laws: Caledon Code (1809) - passes, fixed residence, contracts; apprenticeship of children (1812); Ordinance 50 (1828) - abolished passes, freedom of movement, right to own land and choose employers, equality before the law (campaign by John Philip); Kat River Settlement (1829); slave trade ended 1807-8, abolition 1834.

questions.question: Explain how the frontiers of European settlement expanded in the early nineteenth century.
questions.expected_answer: East: contested Zuurveld; 1812 expulsion of about 20 000 Xhosa across the Fish River; Grahamstown founded as military base; 1820 British settlers; border pushed east through frontier wars (land between the Fish and Keiskamma). North: colonists, traders and missionaries moved to and across the Orange River, meeting the Kora, Griqua and Tswana; mission stations (Griquatown 1803, Kuruman 1816/1824) became centres of trade. Frontiers were zones of co-operation and conflict.
